name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q01 - General molecular formula of alkane homologous series

questiontext.text: Which of the following represents the general molecular formula for the open-chain alkane family (homologous series)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Definition of alkanes
Alkanes are saturated open-chain hydrocarbons containing only carbon-carbon and carbon-hydrogen single bonds.

Step 2: Examine homologous series members
Starting from methane (\(\mathrm{CH}_4\)) where \(n = 1\), ethane (\(\mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_6\)) where \(n = 2\), and propane (\(\mathrm{C}_3\mathrm{H}_8\)) where \(n = 3\), each successive homologue differs by a \(-\mathrm{CH}_2-\) unit.

Step 3: Derive the general formula
For \(n\) carbon atoms, the number of hydrogen atoms required to satisfy carbon tetravalency in an open chain is \(2n + 2\). Thus, the general formula is \(\mathrm{C}_n\mathrm{H}_{2n+2}\).

Final Conceptual Conclusion: The general molecular formula for acyclic alkanes is \(\mathrm{C}_n\mathrm{H}_{2n+2}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q02 - Geometry and bond angle of methane

questiontext.text: According to VSEPR theory, what is the spatial geometry and the \(\mathrm{H-C-H}\) bond angle in a methane molecule?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the hybridisation of carbon in methane
In methane (\(\mathrm{CH}_4\)), the central carbon atom forms four equivalent \(\sigma\) bonds with four hydrogen atoms by head-on overlapping of \(sp^3\) hybrid orbitals with hydrogen \(1s\) orbitals.

Step 2: Determine spatial geometry
Four equivalent electron pairs arrange themselves at the vertices of a regular tetrahedron to minimize mutual electrostatic repulsion.

Step 3: Evaluate the bond angle
In a regular tetrahedron with four identical bonded atoms and no lone pairs, all \(\mathrm{H-C-H}\) bond angles are exactly \(109.5^\circ\).

Final Conceptual Conclusion: Methane possesses a tetrahedral geometry with bond angles of \(109.5^\circ\).

answer.text: Square planar geometry with bond angles of \(90^\circ\)
Trigonal pyramidal geometry with bond angles of \(107^\circ\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q03 - Historical origin of the term olefins

questiontext.text: Alkenes were historically known as 'olefins' because the first member of the series, ethylene, possesses which characteristic property?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Recall the historical name of alkenes
Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons containing carbon-carbon double bonds and were traditionally termed olefins, derived from the Latin words 'oleum' (oil) and 'facere' (to make).

Step 2: Identify the experimental basis
The lowest stable alkene, ethene (\(\mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_4\)), reacts with chlorine gas to form an oily liquid product, ethylene dichloride (1,2-dichloroethane).

Step 3: Conclude the defining behavior
Because of the formation of an oily substance upon halogenation, ethene and its family members were named oil-forming or olefins.

Final Conceptual Conclusion: Ethene forms an oily liquid product upon reaction with chlorine.

answer.text: It burns to produce oily residues without soot
It is extracted directly from olive oil
It forms an oily liquid product on reaction with chlorine

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q04 - Relative rate of alkane halogenation reactions

questiontext.text: What is the correct order of reactivity of halogens towards substitution reactions with alkanes?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understand the halogenation process
Alkanes undergo free radical substitution when treated with halogens under light or elevated temperature.

Step 2: Examine halogen bond energies and activation barriers
Fluorine reacts violently and explosively even in the dark because of very low activation energy and highly exothermic steps. Chlorine reacts steadily in diffused sunlight. Bromine reacts more slowly and selectively. Iodination is exceptionally slow and reversible.

Step 3: Arrange in order of decreasing rate
The established rate of reaction decreases from fluorine to iodine: \(\mathrm{F}_2 > \mathrm{Cl}_2 > \mathrm{Br}_2 > \mathrm{I}_2\).

Final Conceptual Conclusion: The order of reactivity of halogens towards alkanes is \(\mathrm{F}_2 > \mathrm{Cl}_2 > \mathrm{Br}_2 > \mathrm{I}_2\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q05 - Chemical composition of soda lime reagent

questiontext.text: In the laboratory decarboxylation of sodium salts of carboxylic acids to yield alkanes, what is the chemical composition of 'soda lime'?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the decarboxylation reaction
Heating the sodium salt of a carboxylic acid with soda lime eliminates carbon dioxide as sodium carbonate, yielding an alkane with one carbon atom less than the parent acid.

Step 2: Recall the constituents of soda lime
Soda lime is prepared as an intimate dry mixture of sodium hydroxide (\(\mathrm{NaOH}\)) and calcium oxide (\(\mathrm{CaO}\)).

Step 3: Understand the role of calcium oxide
Calcium oxide keeps the strongly hygroscopic sodium hydroxide dry and allows solid-phase heating without melting the glass reaction vessel.

Final Conceptual Conclusion: Soda lime is a mixture of sodium hydroxide and calcium oxide (\(\mathrm{NaOH} + \mathrm{CaO}\)).

answer.text: A mixture of sodium hydroxide and calcium chloride (\(\mathrm{NaOH} + \mathrm{CaCl}_2\))
A mixture of sodium carbonate and calcium carbonate (\(\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{CO}_3 + \mathrm{CaCO}_3\))
A mixture of sodium bicarbonate and quick lime (\(\mathrm{NaHCO}_3 + \mathrm{CaO}\))
A mixture of sodium hydroxide and calcium oxide (\(\mathrm{NaOH} + \mathrm{CaO}\))

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q06 - Dihedral angle of eclipsed ethane conformation

questiontext.text: In the eclipsed conformation of ethane, what is the value of the dihedral (torsional) angle between adjacent \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bonds on the two carbon atoms?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Define dihedral angle
The dihedral or torsional angle is the angle of rotation about the carbon-carbon single bond measured between the planes containing the front \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bond and the rear \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bond.

Step 2: Analyse the eclipsed conformation
In the eclipsed conformation, the \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bonds attached to the front carbon atom align directly in front of the \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bonds of the rear carbon atom.

Step 3: Determine the angular value
Because the front and rear bonds lie in identical planes with no angular separation, the dihedral angle is \(0^\circ\).

Final Conceptual Conclusion: The dihedral angle in the eclipsed conformation of ethane is \(0^\circ\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q07 - Qualitative test for unsaturation using bromine

questiontext.text: What visible observation serves as a classic qualitative laboratory test for carbon-carbon unsaturation when an alkene is treated with bromine dissolved in carbon tetrachloride?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the unsaturation test reagent
Bromine in carbon tetrachloride (\(\mathrm{Br}_2 / \mathrm{CCl}_4\)) has an intense reddish-orange colour.

Step 2: Trace the addition reaction
When an alkene is added, electrophilic addition takes place across the carbon-carbon double bond to form a colourless vicinal dibromoalkane.

Step 3: State the visible change
As the molecular bromine is consumed in forming the vicinal dibromide, the reddish-orange colour of the solution is completely discharged (decolourised).

Final Conceptual Conclusion: Decolourisation of the reddish-orange bromine solution indicates the presence of unsaturation.

answer.text: Evolution of dense brown nitrogen dioxide gas
Discharge and decolourisation of the reddish-orange solution
Appearance of a persistent bright yellow flame

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q08 - Geometry and hybridisation of ethyne molecule

questiontext.text: What is the hybridisation of the carbon atoms and the \(\mathrm{H-C-C}\) bond angle in an ethyne (\(\mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_2\)) molecule?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Examine the electronic configuration and hybridisation
In ethyne (\(\mathrm{HC}\equiv\mathrm{CH}\)), each carbon atom forms one \(\sigma\) bond with hydrogen and one \(\sigma\) bond with the adjacent carbon atom using two \(sp\) hybrid orbitals.

Step 2: Examine remaining p-orbitals
The two unhybridised \(2p\) orbitals on each carbon overlap laterally to create two perpendicular \(\pi\) bonds.

Step 3: Determine geometry and bond angle
The two \(sp\) hybrid orbitals are directed linearly at an angle of \(180^\circ\) to each other, giving ethyne a linear structure with \(\mathrm{H-C-C}\) bond angle of \(180^\circ\).

Final Conceptual Conclusion: The carbon atoms in ethyne are \(sp\) hybridised with a bond angle of \(180^\circ\).

answer.text: \(sp\) hybridised with a bond angle of \(120^\circ\)
\(sp^2\) hybridised with a bond angle of \(120^\circ\)
\(sp\) hybridised with a bond angle of \(180^\circ\)
\(sp^3\) hybridised with a bond angle of \(109.5^\circ\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q09 - Addition of chlorine to benzene under ultraviolet

questiontext.text: When benzene reacts with chlorine in the presence of ultraviolet light at \(500\text{ K}\), three chlorine molecules add to form a compound commonly known as:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the reaction conditions
Benzene reacts with three molecules of chlorine (\(\mathrm{Cl}_2\)) under ultraviolet light or sunlight at \(500\text{ K}\) via a free radical addition process.

Step 2: Determine the product formula
The addition of six chlorine atoms across the three formal double bonds destroys the aromatic ring, yielding benzene hexachloride with molecular formula \(\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_6\mathrm{Cl}_6\).

Step 3: Identify the commercial name
This chlorinated cyclohexane derivative is known commercially as benzene hexachloride (BHC), Lindane, or gammaxane.

Final Conceptual Conclusion: The product formed is benzene hexachloride, commonly termed gammaxane.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q10 - Pi electron count of aromatic benzene ring

questiontext.text: According to Hückel's rule of aromaticity, how many delocalised \(\pi\) electrons are present in a neutral benzene ring corresponding to an integer value of \(n = 1\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: State Hückel's rule
For a planar, cyclic, completely conjugated ring system to be aromatic, it must contain \((4n + 2)\) delocalised \(\pi\) electrons, where \(n\) is a non-negative integer (\(n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots\)).

Step 2: Substitute the value of n
For the monocyclic system benzene with \(n = 1\): \[(4 \times 1 + 2) = 6\pi\text{ electrons}\]

Step 3: Verify with electronic structure
Benzene has six \(sp^2\) hybridised carbon atoms, each contributing one electron in an unhybridised \(2p\) orbital, forming a completely delocalised cloud of six \(\pi\) electrons.

Final Conceptual Conclusion: Benzene contains \(6\pi\) delocalised electrons corresponding to \(n = 1\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q11 - Boiling point trends of isomeric pentane molecules

questiontext.text: Which of the following correctly lists the three structural isomers of pentane (\(\mathrm{C}_5\mathrm{H}_{12}\)) in decreasing order of their boiling points?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the isomers of pentane
The three isomeric pentanes are pentane (\(n\)-pentane), 2-methylbutane (isopentane), and 2,2-dimethylpropane (neopentane).

Step 2: Understand the physical factor controlling boiling point
Intermolecular van der Waals attractive forces depend directly upon the surface area of contact between adjacent molecules.

Step 3: Evaluate the effect of branching
As branching increases, the molecular shape becomes increasingly spherical and compact. A sphere has the minimum surface area per unit volume, which reduces the contact area and weakens the intermolecular van der Waals forces.

Step 4: Compare experimental boiling points
Pentane has an unbranched open chain and boils at \(309.1\text{ K}\). 2-Methylbutane has one branch and boils at \(300.9\text{ K}\). 2,2-Dimethylpropane has two branches (spherical symmetry) and boils at \(282.5\text{ K}\).

Final Conceptual Conclusion: The decreasing order of boiling points is pentane > 2-methylbutane > 2,2-dimethylpropane.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q12 - Origin of ethane byproduct in methane chlorination

questiontext.text: During the photochemical chlorination of methane, a small amount of ethane is formed as a byproduct. Which elementary step in the free radical chain mechanism accounts for this observation?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Review the free radical halogenation mechanism
The mechanism involves three distinct stages: chain initiation, chain propagation, and chain termination.

Step 2: Examine the radicals generated during propagation
In propagation step (a), a chlorine free radical abstracts hydrogen from methane: \(\mathrm{CH}_4 + \dot{\mathrm{Cl}} \rightarrow \dot{\mathrm{C}}\mathrm{H}_3 + \mathrm{HCl}\), producing methyl free radicals (\(\dot{\mathrm{C}}\mathrm{H}_3\)).

Step 3: Examine chain termination pathways
Termination occurs when two free radicals combine with each other, consuming active radicals without generating new ones.

Step 4: Identify the specific coupling step
The combination of two methyl free radicals, \(\mathrm{H}_3\dot{\mathrm{C}} + \dot{\mathrm{C}}\mathrm{H}_3 \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{CH}_3\), forms ethane as a chain-terminating byproduct.

Final Conceptual Conclusion: Coupling of two methyl free radicals in a chain termination step yields ethane.

answer.text: Attack of a chlorine radical on a dichloromethane molecule during propagation
Direct reaction between two methane molecules stimulated by ultraviolet light
Combination of two methyl free radicals in a chain termination step
Homolytic cleavage of a carbon-hydrogen bond in chloromethane

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q13 - Stoichiometry of complete alkane combustion reaction

questiontext.text: Based on the general combustion equation for alkanes, how many moles of \(\mathrm{O}_2\) gas are required for the complete stoichiometric combustion of one mole of butane (\(\mathrm{C}_4\mathrm{H}_{10}\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Recall the general alkane combustion equation
The complete balanced combustion of any alkane is given by: \(\mathrm{C}_n\mathrm{H}_{2n+2} + \left(\frac{3n + 1}{2}\right)\mathrm{O}_2 \rightarrow n\,\mathrm{CO}_2 + (n + 1)\,\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\).

Step 2: Identify the value of n for butane
For butane (\(\mathrm{C}_4\mathrm{H}_{10}\)), the number of carbon atoms is \(n = 4\).

Step 3: Calculate the oxygen coefficient
Substitute \(n = 4\) into the stoichiometric oxygen coefficient: \[\frac{3(4) + 1}{2} = \frac{12 + 1}{2} = \frac{13}{2} = 6.5\]

Step 4: Verify with chemical equation
\(\mathrm{C}_4\mathrm{H}_{10}(\mathrm{g}) + \frac{13}{2}\,\mathrm{O}_2(\mathrm{g}) \rightarrow 4\,\mathrm{CO}_2(\mathrm{g}) + 5\,\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}(\mathrm{l})\). Exactly \(\frac{13}{2}\) (or 6.5) moles of \(\mathrm{O}_2\) are consumed.

Final Conceptual Conclusion: Complete combustion of one mole of butane requires \(\frac{13}{2}\) moles of \(\mathrm{O}_2\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q14 - Controlled catalytic oxidation of methane to methanol

questiontext.text: What major product is obtained when methane and dioxygen are heated in a \(2:1\) molar ratio in the presence of a copper tube catalyst at \(523\text{ K}\) and \(100\text{ atm}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify controlled oxidation reactions of methane
Controlled oxidation of methane yields different products depending on the catalyst and reaction conditions.

Step 2: Evaluate the copper catalyst conditions
When a mixture of methane and oxygen is passed through a copper tube at \(523\text{ K}\) under a pressure of \(100\text{ atm}\), controlled partial oxidation takes place: \[2\,\mathrm{CH}_4 + \mathrm{O}_2 \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Cu}/523\text{ K}/100\text{ atm}} 2\,\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{OH}\]

Step 3: Distinguish from molybdenum oxide catalyst
Heating with molybdenum oxide (\(\mathrm{Mo}_2\mathrm{O}_3\)) produces methanal (\(\mathrm{HCHO}\)), whereas copper produces methanol.

Final Conceptual Conclusion: Controlled oxidation of methane over copper at \(523\text{ K}\) and \(100\text{ atm}\) yields methanol.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q15 - Selective permanganate oxidation of tertiary alkanes

questiontext.text: Although alkanes are generally resistant to chemical oxidising agents, 2-methylpropane is oxidised by potassium permanganate (\(\mathrm{KMnO}_4\)) to form:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Analyze the structural features of 2-methylpropane
The structure of 2-methylpropane is \((\mathrm{CH}_3)_3\mathrm{CH}\). It contains three primary methyl groups and one tertiary carbon bonded to a single tertiary hydrogen atom.

Step 2: Recall the reactivity of tertiary C-H bonds towards oxidation
Alkanes ordinarily resist oxidation by common aqueous reagents, but a tertiary hydrogen atom is relatively reactive due to lower bond dissociation energy and greater stability of intermediate species.

Step 3: Identify the oxidation product
Potassium permanganate specifically oxidises the tertiary \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bond into a tertiary alcohol: \[(\mathrm{CH}_3)_3\mathrm{CH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{KMnO}_4} (\mathrm{CH}_3)_3\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{OH}\] The resulting compound is 2-methylpropan-2-ol.

Final Conceptual Conclusion: Oxidation of 2-methylpropane with potassium permanganate produces 2-methylpropan-2-ol.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q16 - Aromatization of hexane to benzene derivatives

questiontext.text: When \(n\)-hexane is heated to \(773\text{ K}\) under a pressure of \(10\text{--}20\text{ atm}\) in the presence of supported oxides of chromium, vanadium, or molybdenum, which conversion occurs?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the reaction type
Heating an open-chain alkane possessing six or more carbon atoms at elevated temperature and pressure over transition metal oxide catalysts supported on alumina is known as aromatization or reforming.

Step 2: Trace the chemical transformations
The process involves two consecutive steps: dehydrogenation (loss of hydrogen molecules) followed by ring closure (cyclisation).

Step 3: Determine the product from n-hexane
For \(n\)-hexane (\(\mathrm{CH}_3(\mathrm{CH}_2)_4\mathrm{CH}_3\)), cyclisation and loss of four hydrogen molecules results in the formation of the aromatic compound benzene (\(\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_6\)).

Final Conceptual Conclusion: Dehydrogenation and cyclisation of \(n\)-hexane produces benzene.

answer.text: Complete oxidation to produce carbon dioxide and water
Thermal cracking to form propene and propane

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q17 - Energy barrier and torsional strain of ethane

questiontext.text: Rotation around the carbon-carbon single bond in ethane is hindered by an energy barrier of approximately \(12.5\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\). This barrier arises predominantly from which factor?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Define the conformational energy barrier in ethane
The staggered conformation of ethane has lower potential energy than the eclipsed conformation by approximately \(12.5\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Analyze the source of instability in the eclipsed form
In the eclipsed conformation, the electron clouds of adjacent \(\mathrm{C-H}\) \(\sigma\) bonds are brought into closest proximity with zero dihedral angle.

Step 3: Identify the strain phenomenon
The repulsive interaction between adjacent bonding electron pairs is termed torsional strain. It is maximized in the eclipsed form and minimized in the staggered form.

Final Conceptual Conclusion: The energy barrier in ethane is due to repulsive interactions between adjacent bonding electron clouds, known as torsional strain.

answer.text: Steric hindrance between large bulky alkyl substituent groups
Electrostatic attraction between opposite formal charges on carbon atoms
Strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding between ethane molecules
Repulsive interactions between electron clouds of adjacent \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bonds (torsional strain)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q18 - IUPAC nomenclature of conjugated diene hydrocarbons

questiontext.text: What is the correct IUPAC name of the branched diene having the structural formula: \[\mathrm{CH}_2 = \mathrm{C}(\mathrm{CH}_3)-\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{CH}_3)=\mathrm{CH}_2\]?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Analyze the parent conjugated diene
The longest continuous carbon chain containing both double bonds consists of four carbon atoms. The parent diene is buta-1,3-diene.

Step 2: Identify and number substituents
Numbering from either end gives the double bonds at locants 1 and 3, and two methyl substituents at locants 2 and 3.

Step 3: Combine prefix and parent chain
The complete systematic IUPAC name is 2,3-dimethylbuta-1,3-diene.

Final Conceptual Conclusion: The IUPAC name of the compound is 2,3-dimethylbuta-1,3-diene.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q19 - Counting sigma and pi bonds in buta-1,3-diene

questiontext.text: How many sigma (\(\sigma\)) bonds and pi (\(\pi\)) bonds are present in a molecule of buta-1,3-diene (\(\mathrm{CH}_2=\mathrm{CH}-\mathrm{CH}=\mathrm{CH}_2\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Count carbon-hydrogen sigma bonds
Buta-1,3-diene has molecular formula \(\mathrm{C}_4\mathrm{H}_6\). Each hydrogen atom forms a single covalent \(\sigma\) bond with carbon, contributing \(6\) \(\mathrm{C-H}\) \(\sigma\) bonds.

Step 2: Count carbon-carbon sigma bonds
The linear four-carbon backbone \(\mathrm{C}_1-\mathrm{C}_2-\mathrm{C}_3-\mathrm{C}_4\) contains \(3\) carbon-carbon \(\sigma\) bonds.

Step 3: Sum total sigma bonds
Total \(\sigma\) bonds = \(6\,(\mathrm{C-H}) + 3\,(\mathrm{C-C}) = 9\) \(\sigma\) bonds.

Step 4: Count pi bonds
Each carbon-carbon double bond contains one \(\pi\) bond. With two double bonds (at \(\mathrm{C}_1=\mathrm{C}_2\) and \(\mathrm{C}_3=\mathrm{C}_4\)), there are \(2\) \(\pi\) bonds.

Final Conceptual Conclusion: Buta-1,3-diene contains 9 sigma bonds and 2 pi bonds.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q20 - Structural requirements for alkene geometrical isomerism

questiontext.text: Which of the following compounds is capable of exhibiting geometrical (cis-trans) isomerism?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: State conditions for geometrical isomerism
An alkene exhibits geometrical isomerism if rotation about the double bond is restricted and each doubly bonded carbon atom is attached to two different atoms or groups (i.e. \(\mathrm{XYC=CXY}\), \(\mathrm{XYC=CXZ}\), or \(\mathrm{XYC=CZW}\)).

Step 2: Examine propene
In propene (\(\mathrm{CH}_2=\mathrm{CH}-\mathrm{CH}_3\)), \(\mathrm{C}_1\) bears two identical hydrogen atoms; hence no geometrical isomerism is possible.

Step 3: Examine 2-methylprop-1-ene
In \(\mathrm{CH}_2=\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{CH}_3)_2\), \(\mathrm{C}_1\) has two hydrogens and \(\mathrm{C}_2\) has two methyl groups; no cis-trans isomerism is possible.

Step 4: Examine but-1-ene
In but-1-ene (\(\mathrm{CH}_2=\mathrm{CH}-\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CH}_3\)), \(\mathrm{C}_1\) bears two identical hydrogen atoms; cannot show cis-trans isomerism.

Step 5: Examine but-2-ene
In but-2-ene (\(\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}=\mathrm{CH}-\mathrm{CH}_3\)), each double-bonded carbon is bonded to one \(-\mathrm{H}\) and one \(-\mathrm{CH}_3\). This allows two distinct spatial configurations: cis-but-2-ene and trans-but-2-ene.

Final Conceptual Conclusion: But-2-ene satisfies the structural requirements and exhibits cis-trans isomerism.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q21 - Dipole moment difference in but-2-ene isomers

questiontext.text: The dipole moment of cis-but-2-ene is \(0.33\text{ D}\), whereas that of trans-but-2-ene is almost zero. What is the fundamental reason for this difference?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understand the polarity of individual bonds
In but-2-ene, \(sp^3\) hybridised methyl carbons are less electronegative than \(sp^2\) hybridised doubly bonded carbon atoms, generating bond dipole vectors directed from \(-\mathrm{CH}_3\) toward \(=\mathrm{CH}-\).

Step 2: Evaluate vector addition in the trans isomer
In trans-but-2-ene, the two \(\mathrm{C-CH}_3\) bond dipoles point in directly opposite directions across the double bond. Their vector sum cancels out completely, resulting in a net dipole moment of zero.

Step 3: Evaluate vector addition in the cis isomer
In cis-but-2-ene, both \(\mathrm{C-CH}_3\) bond dipoles are oriented on the same side of the double bond, reinforcing each other to produce a net resultant dipole moment of \(0.33\text{ D}\).

Final Conceptual Conclusion: In the trans isomer, the two bond dipole moments point in opposite directions and cancel each other, whereas in the cis isomer they reinforce each other.

answer.text: The cis isomer contains stronger covalent bonds than the trans isomer
In trans-but-2-ene the bond dipoles are in opposite directions and cancel, while in cis-but-2-ene they reinforce each other
The cis isomer undergoes rapid spontaneous ionisation in the liquid phase
The trans isomer has higher resonance stabilisation that quenches polarity

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q22 - Stereoselective cis hydrogenation using Lindlar catalyst

questiontext.text: When an internal alkyne such as but-2-yne is partially reduced with dihydrogen in the presence of Lindlar's catalyst, which stereoisomeric product is predominantly formed?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Define Lindlar's catalyst
Lindlar's catalyst consists of palladised charcoal (\(\mathrm{Pd}/\mathrm{C}\)) that has been partially deactivated ('poisoned') with substances such as quinoline or sulphur compounds.

Step 2: Examine the catalytic surface mechanism
Deactivation prevents further reduction of the alkene to an alkane. Dihydrogen adds to the alkyne from the metallic surface via syn-addition (both hydrogen atoms add from the same side of the triple bond).

Step 3: Determine product geometry
Syn-addition of two hydrogen atoms to but-2-yne yields cis-but-2-ene as the stereoselective product.

Final Conceptual Conclusion: Partial reduction using Lindlar's catalyst yields cis-alkenes stereoselectively.

answer.text: An equimolar mixture of cis-but-2-ene and trans-but-2-ene

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q23 - Stereoselective trans alkene synthesis via sodium ammonia

questiontext.text: Reduction of an internal alkyne with sodium metal in liquid ammonia (\(\mathrm{Na} / \text{liquid } \mathrm{NH}_3\)) stereoselectively yields which type of alkene?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the Birch-type reduction of alkynes
Treatment of an alkyne with sodium in liquid ammonia involves dissolving metal reduction via single electron transfer steps.

Step 2: Analyze the intermediate geometry
Transfer of electrons forms a radical anion intermediate that adopts the trans configuration to minimize electrostatic and steric repulsion between the lone pairs/substituents.

Step 3: Determine product stereochemistry
Subsequent protonation yields the thermodynamically more stable trans-alkene stereoselectively.

Final Conceptual Conclusion: Reduction of an internal alkyne with sodium in liquid ammonia produces a trans-alkene.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q24 - Reactivity trends in dehydrohalogenation of alkyl halides

questiontext.text: During the \(\beta\)-elimination (dehydrohalogenation) of alkyl halides with alcoholic potash (\(\text{alc. } \mathrm{KOH}\)), what are the correct reactivity orders with respect to the nature of the halogen atom and the alkyl group?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Recall the nature of dehydrohalogenation
Alkyl halides heated with alcoholic \(\mathrm{KOH}\) eliminate a molecule of hydrogen halide (\(\mathrm{HX}\)) to form an alkene via \(\beta\)-elimination.

Step 2: Evaluate the leaving group ability of halogens
The carbon-halogen bond strength decreases down the halogen group: \(\mathrm{C-I} < \mathrm{C-Br} < \mathrm{C-Cl}\). Iodide is the best leaving group, making the rate order: \(\text{iodine} > \text{bromine} > \text{chlorine}\).

Step 3: Evaluate the stability of transition state across alkyl groups
Elimination from tertiary alkyl halides forms more highly substituted and stable alkenes, and proceeds through lower activation energy. The rate order for alkyl groups is: \(\text{tertiary} > \text{secondary} > \text{primary}\).

Final Conceptual Conclusion: The reactivity orders are iodine > bromine > chlorine for halogens, and tertiary > secondary > primary for alkyl groups.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q25 - Dehalogenation of vicinal dihalides using zinc

questiontext.text: What product is formed when 1,2-dibromopropane is heated with zinc dust in alcohol?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Classify 1,2-dibromopropane

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q30 - Vigorous oxidation products of 2-methylpropene

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q33 - Electronic basis for acidity of terminal alkynes

questiontext.text: Why do terminal alkynes like ethyne and propyne exhibit acidic character by reacting with strong bases like sodium metal or sodamide (\(\mathrm{NaNH}_2\)), whereas ethene and ethane do not?

Step 1: Compare hybridisation states of carbon
Carbon in ethyne is \(sp\) hybridised (50% \(s\)-character), in ethene is \(sp^2\) hybridised (33.3% \(s\)-character), and in ethane is \(sp^3\) hybridised (25% \(s\)-character).

Step 2: Correlate s-character with electronegativity
Electrons in \(s\) orbitals are closer to the atomic nucleus and held more tightly. Therefore, hybrid orbitals with greater \(s\)-character exhibit greater electronegativity: \(sp > sp^2 > sp^3\).

Step 3: Evaluate C-H bond polarization
Because \(sp\) carbon has high electronegativity, it strongly attracts the shared electron pair of the \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bond. This polarizes the bond and enables hydrogen to be released relatively easily as a proton (\(\mathrm{H}^+\)) by strong bases.

Final Conceptual Conclusion: The high 50% s-character of sp hybrid orbitals increases carbon electronegativity, facilitating proton release.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q34 - Catalytic hydration of propyne to carbonyl compounds

questiontext.text: What is the principal organic product obtained when propyne is warmed with dilute sulphuric acid in the presence of mercuric sulphate (\(\mathrm{HgSO}_4 / \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\)) at \(333\text{ K}\)?

Alkynes add one molecule of water across the triple bond in the presence of \(\mathrm{Hg}^{2+}\) catalyst and dilute \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) at \(333\text{ K}\).

Step 2: Apply Markovnikov regioselectivity to propyne
Addition of \(\mathrm{H-OH}\) across \(\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{C}\equiv\mathrm{CH}\) follows Markovnikov's rule: \(\mathrm{OH}\) attaches to the internal carbon possessing fewer hydrogens, and \(\mathrm{H}\) attaches to the terminal carbon, yielding prop-1-en-2-ol: \[\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{C}\equiv\mathrm{CH} + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \xrightarrow[333\text{ K}]{\mathrm{Hg}^{2+}/\mathrm{H}^+} \left[\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{OH})=\mathrm{CH}_2\right]\]

The resulting enol is unstable and undergoes rapid tautomerisation to the thermodynamically favored keto form, propan-2-one (acetone): \[\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{OH})=\mathrm{CH}_2 \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CO}-\mathrm{CH}_3\]

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q38 - Mechanism and limitations of Kolbe electrolytic synthesis

questiontext.text: During Kolbe's electrolytic synthesis using an aqueous solution of sodium ethanoate, which chemical species is liberated at the anode, and why can methane NOT be prepared by this method?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Analyze the electrochemical ionization
In aqueous solution, sodium ethanoate dissociates into acetate ions: \(2\,\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COO}^- \mathrm{Na}^+ \rightleftharpoons 2\,\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COO}^- + 2\,\mathrm{Na}^+\).

Step 2: Examine the anodic reaction
At the anode, two acetate ions lose two electrons to form acetate free radicals, which instantaneously decarboxylate to generate two methyl free radicals and carbon dioxide: \[2\,\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COO}^- \xrightarrow{-2\mathrm{e}^-} 2\,\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COO}^\bullet \rightarrow 2\,\dot{\mathrm{C}}\mathrm{H}_3 + 2\,\mathrm{CO}_2\uparrow\]

Step 3: Trace radical coupling at the anode
Two methyl free radicals combine to produce ethane gas: \(\dot{\mathrm{C}}\mathrm{H}_3 + \dot{\mathrm{C}}\mathrm{H}_3 \rightarrow \mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}_3\uparrow\). Therefore, ethane and \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) are evolved at the anode.

Step 4: Explain why methane cannot be prepared
Because the formation of the alkane requires the dimerization (coupling) of at least two alkyl free radicals, the resulting alkane must contain a minimum of two carbon atoms. A one-carbon alkane like methane cannot be formed by radical coupling.

Final Conceptual Conclusion: Ethane and carbon dioxide are liberated at the anode; methane cannot be prepared because alkane formation requires coupling of at least two alkyl radicals.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q40 - Conformational stability of ethane in Newman projections

questiontext.text: In the Newman projection of ethane, why is the staggered conformation significantly more stable than the eclipsed conformation?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Analyze bond arrangements in Newman projections
In Newman projections, the front carbon is represented as a point and the rear carbon as a circle. Each bears three \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bonds inclined at \(120^\circ\).

Step 2: Compare the staggered and eclipsed geometries
In the staggered conformation, the dihedral angle between adjacent \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bonds is \(60^\circ\), placing the bonding electron clouds at maximum possible spatial separation. In the eclipsed conformation, the dihedral angle is \(0^\circ\), aligning adjacent \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bonds in direct line with each other.

In the staggered form, maximum distance between electron clouds ensures minimum repulsive forces, lowest potential energy, and maximum molecular stability. In the eclipsed form, closer proximity creates maximum torsional strain, raising potential energy by \(12.5\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).

Final Conceptual Conclusion: The staggered form has maximum separation between bonding electron clouds, leading to minimum torsional strain and maximum stability.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q41 - Bond enthalpy analysis of carbon-carbon double bonds

questiontext.text: The carbon-carbon double bond enthalpy in ethene is \(681\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\), whereas the single bond enthalpy in ethane is \(348\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\). Which analysis correctly accounts for the relative strengths of the \(\sigma\) and \(\pi\) components of the double bond?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understand orbital overlap in a double bond
A carbon-carbon double bond consists of one \(\sigma\) bond formed by head-on overlapping of \(sp^2\) hybrid orbitals and one \(\pi\) bond formed by lateral (sideways) overlapping of unhybridised \(2p\) orbitals.

Step 2: Compare overlap efficiency
Head-on overlap of \(sp^2\) hybrid orbitals occurs along the internuclear axis, achieving high electron density between nuclei and yielding a strong \(\sigma\) bond (bond enthalpy approximately \(397\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)).

Step 3: Evaluate lateral overlap
Sideways overlap between parallel \(2p\) orbitals is substantially less effective, resulting in a significantly weaker \(\pi\) bond (bond enthalpy approximately \(284\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)).

Step 4: Conclude reactivity implications
Although the total double bond enthalpy (\(681\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)) exceeds that of a single bond (\(348\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)), the \(\pi\) bond itself is weaker than the \(\sigma\) bond, making alkenes prone to electrophilic addition.

Final Conceptual Conclusion: The double bond consists of one strong sigma bond (approx 397 kJ/mol) and one weaker pi bond (approx 284 kJ/mol) due to poor lateral overlap.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q43 - Oxidative cleavage of symmetrical but-2-ene

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q44 - Deducing alkene structure from ozonolysis fragments

Step 1: Analyze Kekulé's two contributing structures for o-xylene
In one Kekulé form (I), a double bond is located between the two methyl-bearing ring carbons (\(\mathrm{C}_1=\mathrm{C}_2\)). In the other Kekulé form (II), a single bond connects the two methyl-bearing carbons (\(\mathrm{C}_1-\mathrm{C}_2\)).

Step 2: Predict ozonolysis products from Form I
Cleavage of Form I (with \(\mathrm{C}_1=\mathrm{C}_2\)) cleaves the bond between methyl carbons, yielding one molecule of dimethylglyoxal (\(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COCOCH}_3\)) and two molecules of glyoxal (\(\mathrm{OHC-CHO}\)).

Step 3: Predict ozonolysis products from Form II
Cleavage of Form II (with \(\mathrm{C}_1-\mathrm{C}_2\)) retains the single bond between the methyl groups, yielding two molecules of methylglyoxal (\(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COCHO}\)) and one molecule of glyoxal (\(\mathrm{OHC-CHO}\)).

Step 4: Conclude the theoretical implication
If only one static Kekulé structure existed, dimethylglyoxal and methylglyoxal could not both be produced simultaneously. The isolation of all three carbonyl products in an experimental ratio of \(3:2:1\) confirms that benzene exists as a dynamic hybrid of both oscillating forms.

Final Conceptual Conclusion: The formation of both dimethylglyoxal and methylglyoxal confirms that the double bonds oscillate between adjacent ring carbons, demonstrating resonance.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q46 - Comprehensive acidity order among hydrocarbon classes

questiontext.text: Which of the following correctly arranges the given hydrocarbons in strictly decreasing order of their acidic behaviour?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Analyze hybridization effect across hydrocarbon classes
The percentage of \(s\)-character controls carbon electronegativity and proton release: ethyne (\(sp\), 50% \(s\)) > ethene (\(sp^2\), 33.3% \(s\)) > ethane (\(sp^3\), 25% \(s\)). Hence: \(\mathrm{HC}\equiv\mathrm{CH} > \mathrm{CH}_2=\mathrm{CH}_2 > \mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}_3\).

Step 2: Analyze substitution effects among alkynes
In ethyne (\(\mathrm{HC}\equiv\mathrm{CH}\)), both hydrogens are terminal and directly attached to \(sp\) carbons. In propyne (\(\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{C}\equiv\mathrm{CH}\)), the electron-donating inductive effect (+I) of the methyl group slightly reduces the acidity of the remaining acetylenic hydrogen. In but-2-yne (\(\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{C}\equiv\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{CH}_3\)), there are no hydrogens attached to \(sp\) carbons, so it has no acetylenic acidic hydrogens.

Step 3: Synthesize the comprehensive acidity sequence
Combining these principles gives: \(\mathrm{HC}\equiv\mathrm{CH} > \mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{C}\equiv\mathrm{CH} > \mathrm{CH}_2=\mathrm{CH}_2 > \mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}_3\).

Final Conceptual Conclusion: The decreasing order of acidity is \(\mathrm{HC}\equiv\mathrm{CH} > \mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{C}\equiv\mathrm{CH} > \mathrm{CH}_2=\mathrm{CH}_2 > \mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}_3\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q47 - Stepwise dehydrohalogenation of vicinal dihalides to alkynes

questiontext.text: In the conversion of 1,2-dibromoethane to ethyne, why is the second dehydrohalogenation step carried out using sodamide (\(\mathrm{NaNH}_2\)) rather than alcoholic \(\mathrm{KOH}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Analyze the first elimination step
1,2-Dibromoethane reacts readily with alcoholic \(\mathrm{KOH}\) via \(\beta\)-elimination to lose one molecule of \(\mathrm{HBr}\), forming bromoethene (vinyl bromide, \(\mathrm{CH}_2=\mathrm{CHBr}\)).

Step 2: Examine the structure and bonding in bromoethene
In bromoethene, the unshared lone pairs on the bromine atom conjugate with the \(\pi\) electrons of the double bond: \(\mathrm{CH}_2=\mathrm{CH}-\ddot{\mathrm{Br}}: \leftrightarrow \bar{\mathrm{C}}\mathrm{H}_2-\mathrm{CH}=\stackrel{+}{\mathrm{Br}}\). This gives the carbon-bromine bond partial double bond character.

Step 3: Evaluate the base strength required for the second elimination
Because of partial double bond character and \(sp^2\) hybridization of the carbon, the \(\mathrm{C-Br}\) bond is much stronger and less reactive. Alcoholic \(\mathrm{KOH}\) is not a sufficiently strong base to eliminate the second \(\mathrm{HBr}\) molecule. Sodamide (\(\mathrm{NaNH}_2\)), a much stronger base containing the strongly basic amide ion (\(\mathrm{NH}_2^-\)), is required to achieve elimination and generate ethyne.

Final Conceptual Conclusion: Vinyl bromide possesses resonance-induced partial double bond character in the C-Br bond, requiring the stronger base sodamide for elimination.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q48 - Aromaticity of non-benzenoid cyclic ions

questiontext.text: Why are the cyclopentadienyl anion (\(\mathrm{C}_5\mathrm{H}_5^-\)) and the cycloheptatrienyl cation (tropylium ion, \(\mathrm{C}_7\mathrm{H}_7^+\)) classified as aromatic species?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluate the criteria for aromaticity
According to Hückel's rule, a monocyclic species is aromatic if it is planar, completely conjugated around the ring, and contains \((4n + 2)\) \(\pi\) electrons.

Step 2: Examine cyclopentadienyl anion
The five-membered ring contains two double bonds (\(4\pi\) electrons) and one carbanionic carbon carrying an unshared electron pair in a \(p\) orbital (\(2\pi\) electrons). The entire five-carbon ring is planar and \(sp^2\) hybridized with complete cyclic delocalization of \(4 + 2 = 6\pi\) electrons (\(n = 1\)).

Step 3: Examine cycloheptatrienyl cation (tropylium ion)
The seven-membered ring contains three double bonds (\(6\pi\) electrons) and one positively charged carbon with an empty \(p\) orbital (\(0\pi\) electrons). The ring is planar and completely conjugated with \(6\pi\) electrons, corresponding to \(n = 1\) in \(4n + 2\).

Step 4: Conclude classification
Both non-benzenoid ions are planar, fully conjugated, and possess a Hückel closed shell of \(6\pi\) electrons.

Final Conceptual Conclusion: Both species are planar, cyclic, completely conjugated, and contain \(6\pi\) electrons conforming to \(4n + 2\) with \(n = 1\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q49 - Carbocation rearrangement in Friedel-Crafts propylation

questiontext.text: When benzene is treated with 1-chloropropane in the presence of anhydrous aluminium chloride (\(\mathrm{AlCl}_3\)), the major product obtained is isopropylbenzene (cumene) rather than \(n\)-propylbenzene. What is the fundamental mechanism responsible for this product?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Trace generation of the initial carbocation
Reaction of 1-chloropropane with the Lewis acid \(\mathrm{AlCl}_3\) generates a primary \(n\)-propyl carbocation: \[\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{Cl} + \mathrm{AlCl}_3 \rightarrow \mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{CH}_2^+ + [\mathrm{AlCl}_4]^-\]

Step 2: Analyze carbocation rearrangement
The primary propyl carbocation is relatively unstable. It rapidly undergoes a 1,2-hydride shift from \(\mathrm{C}_2\) to \(\mathrm{C}_1\): \[\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{CH}_2^+ \xrightarrow{1,2-\text{hydride shift}} \mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}^+-\mathrm{CH}_3\]

Step 3: Evaluate carbocation stability
The resulting secondary isopropyl carbocation is much more stable than the primary carbocation due to greater hyperconjugation and inductive stabilisation.

Step 4: Determine electrophilic attack on benzene
Electrophilic substitution of benzene by the predominant isopropyl carbocation yields isopropylbenzene (cumene) as the major product.

Final Conceptual Conclusion: The primary propyl carbocation undergoes a 1,2-hydride shift to form a more stable secondary carbocation before electrophilic attack.

Anhydrous aluminium chloride isomerises the benzene ring into a five-membered intermediate
The primary propyl carbocation undergoes a 1,2-hydride shift to form the more stable secondary isopropyl carbocation

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q50 - Acid-base roles in generating the nitronium electrophile

questiontext.text: In the generation of the active electrophile (nitronium ion, \(\mathrm{NO}_2^+\)) during the nitration of benzene with a mixture of concentrated nitric acid and concentrated sulphuric acid, what are the respective chemical roles of \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) and \(\mathrm{HNO}_3\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Examine the nitrating mixture components
Nitration utilizes a mixture of concentrated \(\mathrm{HNO}_3\) and concentrated \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) (nitrating mixture).

Step 2: Trace proton transfer
Concentrated sulphuric acid is a stronger acid than nitric acid. Therefore, \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) donates a proton (acting as an acid) to the hydroxyl oxygen of nitric acid: \[\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4 + \mathrm{HNO}_3 \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H}_2\stackrel{+}{\mathrm{O}}-\mathrm{NO}_2 + \mathrm{HSO}_4^-\] Here, \(\mathrm{HNO}_3\) accepts the proton, thus acting as a Brønsted-Lowry base.

Step 3: Trace water elimination to generate electrophile
The protonated nitric acid eliminates a water molecule to generate the linear nitronium ion: \[\mathrm{H}_2\stackrel{+}{\mathrm{O}}-\mathrm{NO}_2 \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} + \mathrm{NO}_2^+\]

Step 4: Conclude the acid-base character
In this equilibrium, sulphuric acid serves as the acid and nitric acid serves as the base.

Final Conceptual Conclusion: Sulphuric acid acts as an acid (proton donor) and nitric acid acts as a base (proton acceptor).

Sulphuric acid acts as a reducing agent and nitric acid acts as an oxidising agent
Sulphuric acid acts as an acid and nitric acid acts as a base

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q51 - Structural characteristics of the arenium ion intermediate

questiontext.text: During the electrophilic aromatic substitution of benzene, an electrophile (\(\mathrm{E}^+\)) attacks the ring to form a carbocation intermediate (arenium ion or \(\sigma\)-complex). Which of the following statements correctly describes this intermediate?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Analyze the initial electrophilic attack
When \(\mathrm{E}^+\) attacks a carbon of the benzene ring, two \(\pi\) electrons form a new \(\mathrm{C-E}\) \(\sigma\) bond.

Step 2: Identify the hybridisation of the attacked carbon
The carbon atom that binds the electrophile now has four \(\sigma\) bonds and no \(\pi\) bonds, changing its hybridisation from \(sp^2\) to \(sp^3\).

Step 3: Evaluate resonance delocalization
The positive charge is delocalised over the remaining five \(sp^2\) hybridised ring carbon atoms (specifically at positions ortho and para to the \(sp^3\) carbon).

Step 4: Evaluate aromaticity of the arenium ion
Because delocalisation is interrupted at the tetrahedral \(sp^3\) carbon atom, the \(\sigma\)-complex temporarily loses its continuous cyclic aromatic conjugation.

Final Conceptual Conclusion: The arenium ion contains one sp3 hybridised carbon atom, temporarily loses its aromaticity, and is resonance-stabilised over five carbon atoms.

All six ring carbon atoms remain strictly \(sp^2\) hybridised and maintain continuous aromatic delocalisation
It is an antiaromatic planar species possessing eight delocalised \(\pi\) electrons

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q52 - Directive influence and reactivity of halogenated arenes

questiontext.text: In the electrophilic substitution of chlorobenzene, why does chlorine direct the incoming electrophile to ortho and para positions despite being a deactivating group?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Analyze the inductive effect of chlorine
Chlorine is more electronegative than carbon and exerts a powerful electron-withdrawing inductive effect (-I). This withdraws electron density from the entire ring, lowering overall reactivity towards electrophiles compared to benzene (deactivation).

Step 2: Analyze the resonance effect of chlorine
Chlorine possesses unshared electron pairs that can participate in resonance (+R effect) with the aromatic \(\pi\) system, creating partial double bond character: \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-Cl} \leftrightarrow \text{ortho/para carbanionic canonical forms}\).

Step 3: Compare electron densities at different ring positions
Resonance increases electron density selectively at the ortho and para positions relative to the meta position. When an electrophile attacks at ortho or para positions, the resulting arenium ion is stabilized by additional resonance contribution from chlorine lone pair delocalization.

Step 4: Synthesize reactivity versus orientation
The strong inductive effect (-I) predominates in determining overall reactivity (making chlorobenzene deactivated), but the resonance effect (+R) controls the orientation, directing incoming electrophiles to ortho and para positions.

Final Conceptual Conclusion: The strong -I effect deactivates the ring, but the +R resonance effect stabilizes ortho and para transition states, directing substitution to those positions.

The \(+I\) inductive effect activates the ring while steric hindrance blocks the meta position
